summary: This informational document analyzes the TCP-based routing protocols BGP, LDP, PCEP, and MSDP against the guidelines in Section 4.2 of the KARP design guide, RFC 6518. It examines how well each handles keying and authentication.

plainLanguage.summary: This checks how well several routing protocols guard their secrets and who they talk to, and notes where they fall short.

questions: karp analysis of bgp ldp pcep msdp
is tcp md5 secure for bgp
subtitle: A gap analysis of how BGP, LDP, PCEP and MSDP protect their sessions, measured against the KARP design guide.

tldr.problem: Core routing protocols are an attractive attack target, yet BGP, LDP, PCEP and MSDP rely on weak or manually keyed protection for their TCP sessions, and LDP discovery has none.
tldr.mechanism: The document assesses the current security method of each protocol, describes the optimal state under the KARP design guidelines (RFC 6518), and lists the gaps: key management, key rollover, algorithm agility and replay protection.
tldr.outcome: It is an analysis, not a specification. It points toward TCP-AO and automated key management, plus authentication for LDP Hello messages, as the improvements needed.

today: RFC 6952 is an Informational document and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a snapshot of May 2013: it describes TCP-AO as newly published and the LDP Hello authentication proposal as work in progress.

sections.title: Why Analyze These Protocols
sections.content:
The IAB workshop report in RFC 4948 called an attack on core routing infrastructure an ideal attack. One of its four steps for tightening defenses was to secure the routing protocols' packets on the wire.

RFC 6952 therefore performs an initial analysis of four TCP-based protocols: BGP (RFC 4271), LDP (RFC 5036), PCEP (RFC 5440) and MSDP (RFC 3618). It follows Section 4.2 of the KARP Design Guidelines (RFC 6518), which asks for the current state, the optimal state and the gap between them. It builds on RFC 6039 and on the OSPF analysis in RFC 6863.
sections.plainLanguage: The people who built the internet worried that someone could trick the routers that decide where traffic goes. This paper checks four of those routers' languages for weak locks.

sections.title: Current State: Transport and Keys
sections.content:
Routing protocols already defend themselves with access lists that accept packets only from known sources, and eBGP edge routers run TCP LISTEN only on interfaces where peers are expected. The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (RFC 5082) and the TCP robustness advice in RFC 5961 add more. Even so, sessions remain vulnerable to spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks.

TCP MD5 (RFC 2385) has been obsoleted by TCP-AO (RFC 5925) but is still widely used for BGP. The document calls its MAC too weak, both because of the hash function and the way the secret key is managed. It has no key rollover mechanism and no algorithm agility.

TCP-AO and its algorithms document (RFC 5926) require two MAC algorithms, HMAC-SHA-1-96 and AES-128-CMAC-96, so it supports algorithm agility. But TCP-AO has no key management protocol: the Master Key Table is configured manually or out of band. The document notes that most routers with static keys have never had the key changed, because coordinating a change between pairs of routers is hard. IKEv2 (RFC 5996) is named as a possible way to negotiate TCP-AO keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Many routers still use an old padlock and nobody ever changes the key because it is a hassle. A newer lock exists, but you still have to hand out the keys by hand.

sections.title: Protocol by Protocol
sections.content:
Each protocol has a different weak spot.

  • BGP runs entirely over TCP, so its session security is the transport security above. Securing the routing data itself is handled by the SIDR working group (RFC 6480).
  • LDP Hello messages are sent over UDP, so they get none of TCP's protections. A spoofed Hello with a small Hold Time, or a different Transport Address, can tear down an adjacency or session, and the document says spoofed Hellos have been seen as a real problem in production networks. Session messages use TCP MD5, which is too weak, so a move to TCP-AO is suggested.
  • PCEP can be attacked by spoofing, snooping, falsification and denial of service. RFC 5440 mandated TCP MD5 support because TCP-AO was not yet complete; with TCP-AO now published, new PCEP implementations should fully support it. PCE discovery is another problem, since a discovered PCE has no pre-configured key.
  • MSDP also uses TCP MD5, which is not considered strong enough, and limits the number of cached (S,G) entries to resist state explosion.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router language has its own weak spot. One shouts its greeting in a way anyone can fake, and the others use the old padlock.

sections.title: Optimal State and Gaps
sections.content:
The optimal state is that the protocols withstand all known attack types and support algorithm agility, meaning they are not hard-wired to one algorithm. A key management protocol should negotiate unique, pair-wise random keys and security association parameters including lifetimes, and renew keys before they expire, all without administrator involvement. Keys should change immediately after a breach, such as an administrator with knowledge of the keys leaving the company. Routing information in the payload should also be authenticable.

The gap analysis finds that routers lack comprehensive key management. It describes two kinds of automatic key rollover: implicit rollover, triggered after a volume of data or elapsed time and needing no signaling, and explicit rollover, which needs out-of-band signaling and can be triggered by either side. It also requires replay protection that cannot be defeated by capturing packets and waiting for replay state to be lost. For LDP the proposal in the Hello Cryptographic Authentication work in progress is a new Cryptographic Authentication TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The ideal is a lock that swaps its own key every so often, without a person having to remember. Today people have to change keys by hand, so they never do.

sections.title: Transition and Security Considerations
sections.content:
New mechanisms must support incremental deployment, since changing every router overnight is not feasible. Both ends normally have to agree on a mechanism; if they cannot, setup fails or is deferred and the routers can fall back to what they used before, such as static keys, configurable per node or per interface. Policies can retry the upgrade later.

For security, the protocols need protection from on-path and off-path blind attacks, ideally with a per-packet cryptographic MAC, which in turn needs keys. They need algorithm agility because algorithms weaken over time, and they need key rollover covering both manual and automatic cases, starting from the existing mechanisms that identify the key in a protocol field.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot change all the locks in the world in one night, so the new lock has to work alongside the old one while everyone upgrades.
